newsitem.title: USA: Soybean processor basis higher on supply, margin.
newsitem.headline: Soybean processor basis higher on supply, margin.

text.p: Slow farmer selling and the resulting drop in the amount of soybeans available in cash markets have helped boost basis bids at U.S. crushing plants significantly over the past week, processors and cash sources said.

"Every red-blood American farmer has been attending to the more pressing issue of getting his crops planted," said Jim Quinton, grain merchandiser with Consolidated Grain and Barge in Mt. Vernon, Ind.
"He (the farmer) has not been hauling any soybeans to market," he said.
Because of the drop in available soybeans, crushers have had to raise basis values sharply to attract fresh sales.

Last Monday, the soybean processor basis bid in Decatur, Ill. was quoted at eight cents per bushel over Chicago Board of Trade July futures, and Tuesday basis was quoted at 13 cents per bushel over July, cash sources said.
At a soybean processing plant in Morristown, Ind., the basis climbed to 14 cents over July from 10 cents over, sources said.

"There's no beans out there," said a north-central Indiana processor. "All the ownership is in the country, but without the board rallying, the only way to generate any movement is to jack your basis sky-high."

CBOT July soybean prices have fallen steadily since a contract high of $9.02 per bushel was made on May 7. The falling soybean prices have left farmers with little incentive to sell because most are convinced that the market will eventually rebound to new highs, cash sources said.
"We've lost about 30 to 40 cents (per bushel) in about ten days of so," Quinton said.
"Farmers are convinced that we're going to make it back up to $10.00 (per bushel)," he said.
Some processors said the jump in basis should be attributed to a recent improvement in soybean crush margins.
"The margins have improved, and people have been more willing to jump in there and buy some beans," said one crusher in the U.S. southeast. "People now have an opportunity to make a little money."
Tight supplies of soybeans will continue to keep basis levels firm at least through the summer, Quinton said.
"It will probably ebb and flow as an issue, but from here on out until harvest we'll revist this same situation, Quinton said.

After the Midwest corn and soybean crops are planted, the next noticeable tightening of soybean supplies will likely occur when farmers begin to harvest soft red winter wheat in mid-June, Quinton said.
